main.text: [II, 739] ON THE ANIMALS OF SCRIPTURE [col. 161] PART TWO BOOK TWO ON ON THE UNCLEAN BIRDS.
CHAPTER I.
The eagle, king of the birds; its name, beak, talons, plumage, baldness, renewal, colour.

In this book we shall set out the unclean birds in the same order as Moses in Lev 11:13 and Deut 14:2. First of all is the eagle. To this pertains what Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah] has here: פתח בנשר שהוא מלך בעופות, He began with the eagle, because it is king of the birds. That is, in the list of those birds whose eating God forbade the Jews, he holds that the eagle rightly leads the line, since the consensus of nations has given it kingship over the other birds because of the outstanding gifts by which it surpasses them. As to the Greeks the matter is plain. For Pindar, Olymp. 13, calls the eagle
— — οἰωνῶν βασιλῆα [oiōnōn basilēa],
king of the birds. And Pyth. 1:
Διὸς αἰετὸν, ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν [Dios aieton, archon oiōnōn],
the eagle of Jupiter, leader of the birds. And Isthm. 6:
— — — ἀρχὸν οἰωνῶν μέγαν αἰετὸν [archon oiōnōn megan aieton],
the prince of the birds, the great eagle. And the oracle about the Athenians in the Knights [col. 162] of Aristophanes, Act 3:
Αἰετὸς ὡς γίνει, καὶ πάσης γῆς βασιλεύσεις [Aietos hōs ginei, kai pasēs gēs basileuseis],
Be like an eagle, and you will rule the whole world. Nicander too, where he speaks of the fight of the eagle and the serpent, Theriaca, line 448:
[II, 740] Τῷ μέν τ᾽ ἔκπαγλον κοτέων βασιλήϊος ὄρνις Αἰετὸς, — — — — — — [Tō men t᾽ ekpaglon koteōn basilēios ornis Aietos]

But against him the royal bird, the eagle, raging in monstrous fashion. And Boeus, in book 1 of the Ornithogonia, on Periphas, changed by Jupiter into an eagle: Ποιεῖ γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ὄρνισι βασιλέα [Poiei gar auton en pasi tois ornisi basilea]. For he makes him king among all the birds. And Dionysius in the Bassarica, cited by Stephanus under Κάσπειρος [Kaspeiros]:
Αἰετὸς εἰν ὄρνισι μεταπρέπει ἀγρομένοισιν [Aietos ein ornisi metaprepei agromenoisin],
The eagle excels among the wild birds. And Quintus Smyrnaeus, book 3, line 353:
Αἰετὸς οἰωνῶν προφερέστατος [Aietos oiōnōn propherestatos],
The eagle, most excellent of birds. And Oppian, Halieutica, book 2, line 539:
Ὅσσον γὰρ κέφοισι μετ᾽ οἰωνοῖσιν ἄνακτες Αἰετοί. — — — — — — [Hosson gar kephoisi met᾽ oiōnoisin anaktes Aietoi]

As much as among the light birds the eagles, their kings (excel). And Aelian, Hist. book 9, ch. [col. 163] 2: Τὸν ἀετὸν, τὸν τῶν ὀρνίθων βασιλέα, οὐ μόνον παρόντα, καὶ ζῶντα δέδοικε τὰ ὄρνεα [Ton aeton, ton tōn ornithōn basilea, ou monon paronta, kai zōnta dedoike ta ornea]; The birds fear the eagle, king of the birds, not only when it is alive and present. Finally Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] calls it πτηνοκράτορα [ptēnokratora], that is, prince of the birds. And Tzetzes, Chiliad. 5, Hist. 9, denies that either eagles or lions touch carrion, since they are kings, the former of birds, the latter of wild beasts. And among the Roman writers, Horace, book 4, Ode 4:
Like the winged minister of the thunderbolt, to whom the king of the gods granted kingship over the wandering birds, etc.
Martial, book 5, Epigram 56:
Tell me whom you carry, queen of the birds.
Apuleius, The Ass, book 6: that royal bird of supreme Jupiter. Claudian, Preface to the Third Consulship of Honorius:
— — both mighty over the birds and heir of the thunderbolt.

That the Egyptians too held the same view is shown by these words of Diodorus in book 1: Τὸν δ᾽ ἀετὸν Θηβαῖοι τιμῶσι, διὰ τὸ βασιλικὸν εἶναι δοκεῖν τοῦτο ζῶον, καὶ τοῦ Διὸς ἄξιον [Ton d᾽ aeton Thēbaioi timōsi, dia to basilikon einai dokein touto zōon, kai tou Dios axion]· The Thebans worship the eagle, because they think this animal is royal and worthy of Jupiter. From there the cult of the eagle had also spread to the Arabs. The Talmudists, in the treatise On Idolatry, ch. 1, fol. 11b: בתי ע״ז קבועין אלו הן בית בל בבבל בית נבו בכורסי תרעתא שבמפג צריפא שבאשקלון נשרא שבערביא, These are the fixed idolatrous [II, 741] temples: the temple of Bel at Babylon, the temple of Nebo at Borsippa, Atergatis at Hierapolis, Venus Urania at Ascalon, and the Eagle in Arabia. Those temples are called fixed whose idols are worshipped on every day of the year, as the Gloss explains. Thus Bel was worshipped at Babylon and Nebo at Borsippa (for instead of בכורסי read בבורסיף). And at Hierapolis Derceto, or Atergatis, whose worship at Hierapolis Lucian describes at length in his book On the Syrian Goddess. Derceto, or Atergatis, is in Hebrew תרעתא Tirgata. And Hierapolis is ממבג Mambeg, as in Arabic منبج [Manbij] Manbeg. In Pliny too the text once read Bambyca and Mambeg, which was altered into Magog. Accordingly in the Talmud one should read שבממבג instead of שבמפג. Further, we know from Herodotus that Venus Urania was held in the highest worship at Ascalon. Hence she seems to be the צריפא שבאשקלון, Tseripha, which is at Ascalon. Why she is called צריפא Tseripha, however, is not quite clear. Unless you think she was named from casting [metal]; for among the Hebrews צרף tsaraph means to cast. Hence the Talmudists' בית נצרפי, house of molten images, that is, a temple of idols. Or from lust, over which she presides. For in Arabic صرف [ṣarafa] tsarapha means to burn with lust, and صارفة [ṣārifa] tsaripha is said of a female dog when she is in heat and burns with lust for the male. It remains for us to speak of the eagle of the Arabs. It was the idol of the Dulkelaites among the Homerites, a very well-known people of Arabia Felix. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī, which Bochart cites like an author]: النسر الصنم كان لذي الكلا بارض حمير [al-nasr al-ṣanam kāna li-Dhī al-Kalāʿ bi-arḍ Ḥimyar] The Eagle was the idol of Dulkela in the land of Humeir, that is, of the Homerites. Evidently among the Arabs too this opinion had prevailed, that the eagle is the chief of the birds. So Muaphius, in the book entitled نفحات الازهار [Nafaḥāt al-azhār] Fragrances of Flowers, attributes this to the impure Muhammad: هبط علي جبرييل فقال يا محمد ان لكل شي سيد فسيد البشر ادم وسيد ولد ادم انت وسيد الروم صحيب وسيد فارس سليمان وسيد [col. 164] الحبش بلال وسيد الشجر السدر وسيد الطير النسر [habaṭa ʿalayya Jabrīl fa-qāla yā Muḥammad inna li-kull shayʾ sayyid fa-sayyid al-bashar Ādam wa-sayyid walad Ādam anta wa-sayyid al-Rūm Ṣuhayb wa-sayyid Fāris Salmān wa-sayyid al-Ḥabash Bilāl wa-sayyid al-shajar al-sidr wa-sayyid al-ṭayr al-nasr] Gabriel came down to me and said: O Muhammad, every thing has its lord. The lord of men was Adam; but you are the lord of the sons of Adam. And the lord of the Greeks is Sahib, and of the Persians Soliman, and of the Abyssinians Bilal. And of trees the connarus, a species of lotus, and of birds the eagle, etc. Now, if one wishes to hear the Hebrews: Josephus, On the Jewish War, book 3, chapter 5, writes that the Romans had the eagle as the standard in the first cohort of the legion because the ἀετὸς [aetos] is βασιλεύς τε οἰωνῶν ἁπάντων, καὶ ἀλκιμώτατος [basileus te oiōnōn hapantōn, kai alkimōtatos], king of all birds, and the strongest. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] on Ezek 17:3: הנשר הוא משל לנבוכדנצר מלך בבל כי הנשר מלך העופות וכן נבוכדנצר היה מלך על כל מלכי הארץ, The eagle there is a figure of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, because, as the eagle is king of the birds, so [II, 742] Nebuchadnezzar was king over all the kings of the earth. Hence in the Masal Kadmoni the thirty-eighth Fable bears this title:
צורת הנשר על מושבו : וסנהדרי׳ העוף יושבים סביבו :

The figure of the eagle upon its throne, and the council of birds sitting around it. That is, in the council of the birds the eagle is depicted, distinguished by a crown and raised high on a throne, and the other birds stand by it. And of the eagle Baal Hatturim says, right at the beginning of this chapter, הוא מלך העופות, It holds kingship over the birds. Finally, the Fathers define the very same thing. Thus Ambrose, Hexaëm. book 5, ch. 18, calls the eagle a royal bird and attributes to it royal eminence. Jerome on Mich. 1: The eagle, which is queen of the birds. And on Dan. VII.: As the lion holds kingship among the beasts, so the eagle among the birds. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, chapter 6: Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ἀετὸς βασιλεὺς τῶν ὀρνέων· [Esti gar ho aetos basileus tōn orneōn] For the eagle is king of the birds, or queen, if you prefer. Theodoret, in the Preface to the Song, on the passage Ezek 17:3: Ἀετὸν μὲν τὸν βασιλέα (ἐνόησεν), ἐπειδὰν καὶ τὸ ζῶον βασιλικόν· [Aeton men ton basilea (enoēsen), epeidan kai to zōon basilikon] By the name of eagle he meant the king, because it is a royal animal. Theodore of Heraclea on Psal. CII.: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ἀετὸς δοκεῖ βασιλεύειν τῶν πετεινῶν ἁπάντων· [Epeidē ho aetos dokei basileuein tōn peteinōn hapantōn] Because the eagle seems to rule over all the birds. And a little later: Διὰ γὰρ τοῦ ὄρνιθος τοῦ ἀετοῦ τὴν βασιλείαν αἰνίττεται, [Dia gar tou ornithos tou aetou tēn basileian ainittetai] For by the eagle he signifies the kingdom. What of the fact that it was commonly believed that the eagle is at war with the wren because the latter καλεῖται πρέσβυς, καὶ βασιλεὺς [kaleitai presbys, kai basileus], is called senator and king, as though it begrudged it this name? So the Philosopher attests, Hist. book 9, ch. 11. Hence Pliny, book 10, ch. 74: The eagle and the wren are at odds, if we believe it, because the latter is called king of the birds.

Whence the eagle, in Hebrew נשר neser, gets its name has so far escaped the masters. For absurd is the fancy of Rabbi Bechai on Gen. II. that it derives from the Chaldee נשר nesar, which means to fall down, because, after it has risen in flight to the element of fire, as they indeed would have it, it then falls headlong into the sea. Nor do I agree with those who assert that it is named from the shedding of its feathers, because נשר among the Rabbis means to fall off; or from sight, because נשר neser seems to allude to the verb שור sur, which means to see. Rather, I most approve of the Arabs, for whom نسر [nasara] nasara means to pluck with the beak, and منسر [minsar] minsar means beak, and properly that of a bird of prey. From this, then, they hold that the eagle is called نسر [nasr] nesr, لانه ينسر الشي ويقتلعه [li-annahu yansiru al-shay wa-yaqtaliʿuhu] because it tears and plucks a thing with its beak. So Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ], Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] and Alcamus. Other birds of prey also pluck with the beak; yet this is ascribed by special right to the prince of the birds of prey, the eagle, [col. 165] because its beak is more hooked and it tears more forcefully with it. Likewise, swooping upon prey is common to all, which in Hebrew is העיט. Hence עיט ajit is in general [II, 743] a bird of prey. Yet usage among the Greeks made ἀετόν [aeton] or αἰετόν [aieton], derived from it, the proper name of the eagle ^{R1}.

The eagle is remarkable not only for its beak but also for its talons, which it has not straight, like a man, but curved and hooked like a lion's. For of the animals that have claws, τὰ μέν εἰσιν εὐθυόνυχα, ὥσπερ ἄνθρωπος· τὰ δὲ γαμψώνυχα, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν πεζῶν λέων, καὶ τῶν πτηνῶν αἰετὸς [ta men eisin euthyonycha, hōsper anthrōpos; ta de gampsōnycha, hōsper kai tōn pezōn leōn, kai tōn ptēnōn aietos], some have straight claws, like man; others hooked, like the lion among land animals and the eagle among birds. So the Philosopher, Hist. book 3, ch. 9. In birds, that is, the talons imitate the shape of the beak. Suidas: Γαμψώνυχα ὅσα τῶν ζώων τὴν ἐπιρυγχίδα γεγάμψωκεν ὑπὸ τὴν γένυν, οἷα ἐστὶν ἀετός· [Gampsōnycha hosa tōn zōōn tēn epirynchida gegampsōken hypo tēn genyn, hoia estin aetos] Those animals have hooked claws which have a beak curved beneath the jaws, to which kind the eagle belongs. The Grammarians are uncertain to which of the two it refers that the eagle which the sleepless Penelope saw is called
— — — μέγας αἰετὸς ἀγκυλοχείλης· [megas aietos ankylocheilēs]

For to some ἀγκυλοχείλης [ankylocheilēs] is ὁ ἔχων ἀγκύλα χείλη, ἤτοι τὸ ῥάμφος [ho echōn ankyla cheilē, ētoi to rhamphos], one that has curved lips, [II, 744] that is, a curved beak; to others ἐπικαμπεῖς τὰς χηλὰς ἔχων [epikampeis tas chēlas echōn], one that has bent talons. In this sense, in Aristophanes' Knights, Cleon is called
— — βυρσαίετος ἀγκυλοχείλης, [byrsaietos ankylocheilēs]
because like an eagle he had hooked or rapacious claws, as not only the Scholiast but also Aristophanes himself explains. And in Plautus' Pseudolus the cook says,
Do you expect to find any cook who has not a kite's or an eagle's talons?

But many of the ancients also believed that in Ezek 17:3 7. the eagle is called מלא הנוצה and רב הנוצה on account of its talons. For this is rendered by the Greeks ὁ ἀετὸς πλήρης ὀνύχων [ho aetos plērēs onychōn], the eagle full of talons, and πολὺς ὄνυξι [polys onyxi], great in talons, or having many talons. The Arabic follows the same. Nor does the Syriac differ much in verse 3, ܡܠܝܢ ܛܦܪ̈ܘܗܝ [מלין טפרוהי], its talons are full, and in verse 7, ܣܓܝܐܢ ܛܦܪܘܗܝ [סגיאן טפרוהי] its talons are many. For them, that is, נוצה is talon. But the Chaldee, Jerome and all the Hebrews more correctly explain it as feather or plumage. Indeed the Greeks themselves in Lev 1:16 have σὺν τοῖς πτεροῖς [syn tois pterois] for בנצתא, and Theodotion σὺν τοῖς πτίλοις [syn tois ptilois]. For נצה means to fly, whence נצו they flew, or flew away, Lam 4:15, and נוצה feather or plumage, which lifts birds up to flight. This suits this passage better. For I, at least, cannot understand what an eagle full of talons, or with many talons, would be, since all eagles have the same number of talons. But an eagle is rightly said to be full of feathers, or to have many feathers, in contrast to the bald one ^{R2}, of which Mic 1:16 speaks: Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle. For at the onset of spring birds of prey are subject to the shedding of their feathers. This we call muer, that is, to change feathers. For so those speak who write on this subject. And this is precisely μουτεύειν [mouteuein] among the Greeks of a later age. Demetrius, Orneosophion, book 2, chapter 53: Ἐὰν δὲ βραδύνῃ εἰς τὸ μουτεῦσαι [Ean de bradynē eis to mouteusai]. Though proper words are not lacking, such as μαδίζεσθαι [madizesthai], πτεροῤῥυῆσαι [pterorrhyēsai], and ἀποβάλλειν τὰ πτερὰ [apoballein ta ptera], which the same writer uses. In Arabic you would say كرز [kariza] curiza. Alcamus: كرز البازي سقط ريشه [kariza al-bāzī saqaṭa rīshuhu] curiza albazi, that is, of the hawk, its plumage fell out. Whence كرز [kurraz] corraz, a hawk, or any bird of prey whose feathers are falling out. Thus in Micah the baldness of the eagle is the time when most of its feathers have dropped out. For although baldness is properly attributed to man, [col. 166] [II, 745] birds too are called bald. Pliny, book 11, chapter 37: Some animals are naturally bald, such as ostriches and water ravens, which among the Greeks take their name from this, that is, οἱ φαλακροκόρακες [hoi phalakrokorakes]. Thus both the Greeks and the Hebrews attribute baldness to birds, differing only in this, that whereas among the Greeks the baldness of birds concerns the head alone, the Hebrews extend it to the whole body; and they call a bird bald which is smooth and stripped of feathers ^{R3}.

But when others have gradually grown in place of the feathers that fell out, then at last the eagle (in Hebrew נשר) is called מלא הנוצה, full of plumage, and רב נוצה, teeming with plumage. And Scripture indicates in more than one place that feathers grow again in eagles. So in the famous passage of David, Psal. CIII, 5. תתחדש כנשר נעוריכי, You will renew your youth like the eagle. I prefer to render it so with the Chaldee rather than with others, Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's, because the verb תתחדש, of the third person, since it is singular and feminine, agrees neither in gender nor in number with נעוריכי, which is plural and masculine. However that may be, youth is renewed in the eagle in no other way than when new feathers succeed the old, just as a serpent is said to shed its old age when it lays aside its old skin. Hence the Greeks call the slough of a serpent γήρας [gēras], the Romans senium [old age] and senectus [old age]. Thus the words of the Psalmist have the same sense as these of Isaiah, chapter 40, verse 31: Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength. They shall mount up (grow) feathers like eagles. Where the Seventy elegantly have Πτεροφυήσουσιν ὡς ἀετοί [Pterophyēsousin hōs aetoi]. But by a strange metamorphosis the Syriac has transformed the eagles into doves in this version of his, ܢܦܩܘܢ ܓܦܐ ܐܝܟ ܕܝܘܢܐ [נפקון גפא איך דיונא], They will put forth wings like those of doves. And by no smaller error eagles have been made lions in these words of Theodotion about king Nebuchadnezzar, Dan 4:30 var. 33. Αἱ τρίχες αὐτοῦ ὡς λεόντων ἐμεγαλύνθησαν [Hai triches autou hōs leontōn emegalynthēsan]. His hairs grew like those of lions. For in the original it is כנשרין, like those of eagles. But this is an error of the scribes, not of the translator. For no doubt the translator had written ἀετῶν [aetōn], which ignorant scribes changed to λεόντων [leontōn] because αἱ τρίχες [hai triches], that is hairs, did not seem able to fit eagles. So they substituted for eagles the name of a hairy animal, but from a pointless scruple. For in the Prophet's words an analogous word could be supplied: His hairs grew like those of eagles, supply feathers, which are in birds what [II, 746] hairs are in men. Moreover, hairs and locks are sometimes attributed even to birds. By this catachresis Oppian, in book 3 of the Cynegetica, says of the hen that sees a hawk gaping after her chicks,
— — — ἑαῖς ἔφριξεν ἐθείραις [heais ephrixen etheirais],
bristled with its hair. And Matron, in the Parodies quoted by Athenaeus in book 14, describes hens served at a banquet,
Ἄτριχας, οἰετέας, λαγάνοις κατὰ νῶτον ἐΐσας, [Atrichas, oieteas, laganois kata nōton eïsas,]

Hairless, equal in age, like flat cakes on the back. Hairless, that is, featherless. Nor is there any need to restore ὄτριχας [otrichas] with Casaubon, because that is the reading in the verse of Homer to which he alludes, Iliad 2, line 765. For the parody [παρῳδία, parōdia] consists precisely in this, that a similar word, not the same one, is substituted. Many examples make this plain. So, just as the feathers of hens are called hairs, so too are those of eagles. Hence Tertullian, near the end of his book On Penitence, speaking of King Nebuchadnezzar: his hair, through neglect, displaying an eagle-like shagginess. For this Pamelius substituted leoninum [lion-like], as if an eagle could not be said to bristle with hair. This is refuted by what we have already shown, that the feathers of birds too are reckoned under the name of hairs. And indeed, since Micah (ch. 1, v. 16) says that eagles grow bald, why could not the Prophet Daniel have attributed hairs to them? Certainly the same catachresis [κατάχρησις, katachrēsis] occurs in both places. For baldness is properly the falling out of the hair of the head. [col. 167] Meanwhile the corruption of the passage of Daniel is not recent, since besides the Arabic translator it is followed by Theodoret on Daniel, by the author of the Questions attributed to Justin, Question 44, and by those who wrote the Lives of the Prophets under the names of Epiphanius and Dorotheus, who, though spurious and pseudonymous [ψευδώνυμοι, pseudōnymoi] writers, are nevertheless fairly ancient. Now, if you compare these three passages, first that of the Psalmist, you will renew your youth like the eagle; second that of Isaiah, For those who hope in the Lord their strength will be restored, their wings will grow again like eagles'; third that of Daniel, His hairs grew like those of eagles ^{R4}: you will see that all of them concern the feathers of eagles, which are restored after moulting [ψίλωσιν, psilōsin]. Hence the eagle comes to seem more vigorous, and so even younger. Nor would it be absurd to join to these the passage of Job about the hawk, chapter 39, verse 26: Is it by your understanding that יאבר נץ, the hawk grows its feathers, spreading its wings toward the south? That is, so that during that moulting [ψιλώσει, psilōsei] it may be revived by the gentle warmth of the sun, and new feathers may more easily grow back in place of those it has lost.

[II, 747] Because many ancient writers did not pay sufficient attention to these points, they invented a great deal about the ἀνακαίνωσις [anakainōsis] and ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of eagles, which it is tedious to report here ^{R5}. Well known is the fiction of Saadia, cited by Kimchi on Psal. CIII. and Es. XL.: הנשר יעוף על כל העופות ויעלה מאד על פני רקיע השמים ויקרוב לחום האש היסודי ויפול עצמו בים מרוב חום ויתחדש ויעלה אבר וישוב לימי עלומיו כן כל עשר עד מאה וכשיגיע למאה יעלה כמנהגו ויפול בים וימות שם, The eagle flies higher than any of the birds and is carried far up towards the firmament, until it comes near the elemental fire. Then, burning with the heat, it throws itself headlong into the sea, and is renewed; its feathers grow again, and it returns to the days of its youth. And this happens every ten years up to the hundredth year; when it has reached that, it is carried upward as usual, falls headlong into the sea, and dies there. Similar is what we read in Porta coeli fol. 22, col. 2: ויש אומרים כי הנשר טבעו לעלות קרוב לגבול האש ומתלהב בסוף עשר שנים לעשר שנים ומרוב חמומו מפיל עצמו בים לקרר חומו ושם ימרט נוצתו ויתחדש נוצה אחרת ויתחדש כחו עד ק׳ שנה שיעלה שם ויפול בים ויטבע, There are some who say that it is natural to the eagle to ascend close to the boundary of fire and to be set ablaze every ten years, and, burning with the heat, to cast itself into the sea to cool that heat; and that there its feathers fall out and others grow in their place, and its strength is restored, up to the hundredth year, when, carried up to the same place, it falls headlong and is drowned in the sea. Others say it is plunged not into the sea but into a spring, and, washed in it, grows young again. Damir, on العقاب [al-ʿuqāb] alokab, that is, περὶ τοῦ μελαναιέτου [peri tou melanaietou] [on the black eagle], which is a kind of eagle especially common in Arabia Felix: متي ثقلت عن النهوض او عميت حملتها الفراخ ونقلتها من مكان الي مكان تلتمس لها عينا صافيتا بارض الهند علي راس جبل فيتغمسها فيها ثم تضعها في شعاع الشمس فيذهب ريشها وينبت لها ريش جديد ويذهب ظلمة بصرها ثم تعوص في تلك العين [matā thaqulat ʿan al-nuhūḍ aw ʿamiyat ḥamalathā al-firākh wa-naqalathā min makān ilā makān taltamisu lahā ʿaynan ṣāfiyatan bi-arḍ al-Hind ʿalā raʾs jabal fa-yataghammasuhā fīhā thumma taḍaʿuhā fī shuʿāʿ al-shams fa-yadhhabu rīshuhā wa-yanbutu lahā rīsh jadīd wa-yadhhabu ẓulmat baṣarihā thumma taʿūṣu fī tilka al-ʿayn] [col. 168] فاذا هي قد عادت شابة [fa-idhā hiya qad ʿādat shābba] And when it becomes slow in flight and goes blind, its chicks carry it and move it from place to place, and in India they seek for it a pure spring on the summit of a mountain; they plunge it into this and set it facing the rays of the sun. Then its feathers fall out and new ones grow for it, and the dimness of its eyes is dispelled; and it is plunged [II, 748] again into the same spring, when its grey age has returned. The author of the Letter to Praesidius, which is attributed to Jerome: When the eagle has grown old, its feathers and eyes become heavy; it seeks a spring, raises its feathers, and gathers heat into itself, and so its eyes are healed; and it plunges itself three times into the spring, and thus returns to youth. Eustathius, on the Hexaëmeron, p. 27: Φασὶ γηράσαντα τὸν ἀετὸν ἀμαυροῦσθαι τὰς ὄψεις, καὶ βαρεῖσθαι αὐτοῦ τὰς πτέρυγας, καὶ εἰς πηγὴν ἀφικνεῖσθαι, καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰθέρα ἀνιπτάμενον, ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου τὰς πτέρυγας καταφλέγεσθαι, καὶ ἀναβλέπειν· εἶθ᾽ εὐθὺς ἐπὶ τὴν πηγὴν καταβάντα τρίτον βαπτίζεσθαι, καὶ ἀνανεοῦσθαι. Διὸ καὶ τὸν Ψαλμὸν φάσκειν φησὶν, Ἀνακαινισθήσεται ὡς ἀετοῦ ἡ νεότης σου. [Phasi gērasanta ton aeton amaurousthai tas opseis, kai bareisthai autou tas pterygas, kai eis pēgēn aphikneisthai, kai eis ton aithera aniptamenon, hypo tou hēliou tas pterygas kataphlegesthai, kai anablepein; eith᾽ euthys epi tēn pēgēn katabanta triton baptizesthai, kai ananeousthai. Dio kai ton Psalmon phaskein phēsin, Anakainisthēsetai hōs aetou hē neotēs sou.] They say that the eagle, worn out by old age, has the sharpness of its eyes dulled and its wings grow heavy, and it makes for a spring; and while it is carried up in flight into the air, its wings are scorched by the sun and it recovers its sight; then, when it comes down into the spring, it is plunged into it three times and renewed. And therefore the Psalm said, „Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's“. An Anonymous writer on the Psalms: Ὁ ἀετὸς κατὰ φ´ ἔτη ἀνακαινίζεται. καιόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου, καὶ καταδυόμενος εἰς πηγὴν ὕδατος, πάλιν νέος εὑρίσκεται. [Ho aetos kata ph´ etē anakainizetai. kaiomenos hypo tou hēliou, kai katadyomenos eis pēgēn hydatos, palin neos heurisketai.] The eagle is renewed every five hundredth year. Scorched by the sun and plunged into a spring of water, it is found young again. Some write ϱ´ [r´], that is, hundredth, instead of φ´ [ph´], that is, five hundredth, so that this writer may agree with Epiphanius, whose words are: Ἀετὸς δὲ καλεῖται διὰ τὴν πολυετίαν αὐτοῦ. οὗτος μὲν ζῇ ἔτη ἑκατὸν, καὶ γηράσαντος γρυποῦται ὁ προμυκτὴρ, καὶ ἀμβλυώττουσιν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτοῦ, τοῦ μὴ ὁρᾷν, καὶ οὐκ ἰσχύει φαγεῖν. ἀνέρχεται δὲ εἰς ὕψος λίαν, καὶ ῥίπτει ἑαυτὸν ἐπὶ ἀκροτόμου πέτρας, προσκρούσας αὐτῇ τὸ ῥάμφος, καὶ λούεται ἐπὶ τὴν ψυγρὰν λίμνην, καὶ κάθηται κατὰ τὸ ἡλιακὸν θερμὸν, πίπτουσι δὲ λεπίδες ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν, καὶ πάλιν εἰς νέους τελεῖν ἄρχεται. [Aetos de kaleitai dia tēn polyetian autou. houtos men zē etē hekaton, kai gērasantos gryproutai ho promyktēr, kai amblyōttousin hoi ophthalmoi autou, tou mē horan, kai ouk ischyei phagein. anerchetai de eis hypsos lian, kai rhiptei heauton epi akrotomou petras, proskrousas autē to rhamphos, kai louetai epi tēn psygran limnēn, kai kathētai kata to hēliakon thermon, piptousi de lepides apo tōn ophthalmōn, kai palin eis neous telein archetai.] The eagle is called ἀετὸς [aetos] on account of its long life. For it lives a hundred years. But when it grows old, its beak becomes hooked and its eyes grow dim, so that it can neither see nor eat. So it rises on high and hurls itself against a sheer rock, against which it strikes its beak; and it washes itself in a cold lake and sits in the heat of the sun; and scales fall from its eyes, and it grows young again. Augustine too, on Psalm 102, writes that the upper beak of an ageing eagle grows so much that the passage for eating is closed. This very thing Aristotle ^{a)}, Pliny ^{b)} and Horapollo ^{c)} expressly teach. But whereas they add that with its beak growing in this way it dies of hunger, Augustine asserts that, having worn down its beak against a rock, it restores its failing strength by eating. Yet lest anyone think this is handed down by him as certain, here are the holy man's words on Psalm LXVI.: Our youth shall be renewed like the eagle, provided only that we wear down our old age against the rock. Whether those things are true, etc., which are said about the eagle, [II, 749] or whether it is rather a report of men than the truth, yet the truth is in the Scriptures, and not without reason have the Scriptures said this. Let us do whatever it signifies, and not trouble ourselves how true it is. Indeed, since the things that the writers we have cited relate about the ἀνανέωσις [ananeōsis] of the eagle are either false or uncertain, let us embrace only what all acknowledge as true and certain: namely, that the eagle at a fixed time casts off its old feathers and then takes on others, and is renewed in this way. Hence the genuine Jerome, on Isaiah chapter 40: We have often said that the old age of eagles grows young again by the changing of their feathers. And Euthymius on Psalm CII.: You will lay aside the feeble old age which diseases and sins had brought on, ὡς ἐκεῖνος τὸ γῆρας τῶν ἑαυτοῦ πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos to gēras tōn heautou pterōn], [col. 169] as it does the old age of its feathers. You will be renewed through repentance, ὡς ἐκεῖνος διὰ τῆς παλιφυΐας πτερῶν [hōs ekeinos dia tēs paliphyias pterōn], as it is through the regrowth of its feathers.

Among the kinds of eagles, many take their name from their colour. Thus the πύγαργος [pygargos] ^{d)} is so called from its whitish tail, the μορφνὸς [morphnos] from its dusky colour, the μελαναίετος [melanaietos] from its black colour, the περκνόπτερος [perknopteros] from the markings of its wings, and the χρυσαίετος [chrysaietos], also called ἀστερίας [asterias], from its golden gleam and from the spots sprinkled over it like stars. To this last I refer these words of Ezek 17:3: A great eagle, with great wings, long pinions, full of plumage, in which was רקמה rekama, that is, Phrygian work. For that this eagle, the ἀστερίας [asterias] or starry eagle, is the largest of the eagles, we learn from these words of Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 39: Ἀκούω δέ τι καὶ γένος ἀετῶν, καὶ ὄνομα αὐτῶν χρυσαίετον ἔθεντο· ἄλλοι δὲ ἀστερίαν τὸν αὐτὸν καλοῦσιν· ὁρᾶται δὲ οὐ πολλάκις, etc. μέγιστος δὲ ἀετῶν εἶναι πεπίστευται. [Akouō de ti kai genos aetōn, kai onoma autōn chrysaieton ethento; alloi de asterian ton auton kalousin; horatai de ou pollakis, etc. megistos de aetōn einai pepisteutai.] I hear that there is also a certain kind of eagle which some call Chrysaetos, others Asterias or the starry eagle. It is not often seen, etc. It is believed to be the largest of the eagles ^{R6}. But I know of no kind of eagle with a blood-red tail, such as the Syriac translator describes in these words at Rev 8:13: And I saw, and heard one eagle flying in the midst, ܕܢܫܪܐ ܕܕܡܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ [דנשרא דדמא אית לה], which had a blood-red tail. So the matter would be stuck here, were the sources of the error not plain. The Greek has μεσουρανήματι [mesouranēmati], that is, in mid-heaven. The translator took this as if he had read ἐν μέσῳ οὐρὰν αἵματι [en mesō ouran haimati], supplying βεβαμμένην ἔχοντος [bebammenēn echontos]: an eagle in the midst, having its tail (supply dyed) with blood, than which nothing more absurd could be devised. On this passage see the Notes of Edward Pococke [=Edward Pococke, Commentary on Hosea (1685)], a man by far the most learned in these studies.

notes.text: That نِسْر [nisr] is today the Arabic name of eagles is also confirmed by Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] in Descriptt. Animall. p. 12. But just as the Arabs often take eagles, نِسْر [nisr], and vultures, رخم [rakham], indiscriminately, and attribute to the eagle many things that are proper to the vulture, as Bochart will show at length below in Chapter XXVII, so it is likely that the Hebrews too sometimes confused birds of both kinds and took one for the other. Medieval writers also confuse vultures with eagles, as Jo. Gottl. Schneider observes on Frederick II, De arte venandi cum avibus, p. 52. "Of eagles," says Leo Africanus, Descript. Afr. book 9, ch. 56, "there are various species, differing in their properties, size and colour: the larger are called Nesir in the Arabic idiom." And in ch. 57: Nesir "is the largest of the birds of Africa; in body it exceeds the crane, yet it is shorter in beak, neck and legs." These marks are rather uncertain and fit more than one bird of the eagle kind. This one thing seems certain: the word نسر [nsr] comprehends birds similar to one another but different in species. Alb. Schultens [=Albert Schultens, Liber Jobi (1737)] rightly says in his Commentary on Job XXXIX, p. 1136: "See Pliny, book 10, ch. 3, where six kinds of eagles are indicated. The name common to all is נשר, نسر [nsr]. The species noted in Scripture are פרס, the ossifrage, and עזניה, the Melanaetos or Valeria." Therefore I cannot agree with Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] [Vermischte Sammlungen, fasc. 1, ch. 5; fasc. 3, p. 164; and fasc. 5, p. 73], who assigns the name נשר to the bearded vulture alone, although I do not think it should be excluded altogether. But most of what is recorded of the נשר in the sacred books fits the whole kind of eagles and vultures. — Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in Supplemm. p. 1695, which should be read, inclines more to the eagle; with him may be compared what a certain learned man notes in the Sylloge of observations on Bruce's [=James Bruce, Travels to discover the source of the Nile (1790)] travels, edited by Hassencamp, p. 161.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: For my part I would think that these words refer rather to the fact that birds of the eagle and vulture kind bear a denser covering of feathers than other birds of prey. There is no adequate reason for referring them specifically to the bearded vulture, with Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 73.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: Oedmann's opinion, vol. 1, p. 64, is that Micah's words allude to the bald back of the head of the bearded vulture, which the head of one who has shorn his hair in mourning resembles. To the objections raised by J. D. Michaelis in the Bibl. Orient. Nova vol. 3, p. 45 ff., he replied in vol. 3, p. 168 ff. The head of the bearded vulture is seen in an illustration at the end of Part 3 of Oedmann's book.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: To Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 73, this passage seems to hint at the shaggy appearance of the bearded vulture, caused by the projecting hair-like feathers on the neck, breast and upper back. I can hardly persuade myself that any particular species of eagle was in the writer's mind.
notes.label: R4

notes.text: This fable perhaps originated from what Leo Africanus relates of the Nesir, book 9, ch. 57, p. 511: "It lives a very long life, and we have seen very many featherless from old age: therefore, when their feathers fall out, they return to the nest, as if newly hatched, and are fed by the younger ones."
notes.label: R5

notes.text: This very eagle, which he had carefully observed, was described most accurately by Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)], Ornithol. vol. 1, book 2, p. 112. There, among other things, he says: "The colour of the wings and tail was dusky, the more so the larger the feathers. That of the other, smaller feathers of the whole body was a rusty or chestnut brown," with white spots scattered here and there, few on the back, more on the belly, the roots everywhere white. "The flight feathers of the wings were six on each side, two spans and a palm long, with very firm and hard quills." You see that Bochart, with every right, refers Ezekiel's words to the ἀστερίας [asterias], which is also the χρυσάετος [chrysaetos], the largest of the eagles. But here too Oedmann, vol. 1, p. 74, sees his bearded vulture.
notes.label: R6
